title.en: What is a function? One-one, onto and constant functions

text.en: You press button B3 on a vending machine and always get the same biscuit. Press it again - same biscuit. A machine that gives exactly one output for each input is behaving like a function.

A function f from A to B is a relation in which every element of A is paired with exactly one element of B.
So no element of A may be left out and no element of A may have two arrows leaving it.
We write y = f(x); x is the independent variable (input) and y the dependent variable (output).
A vertical-line test on a graph checks this: a vertical line must cut the graph at most once.
A function is one-one if different inputs always give different outputs, that is f(a) = f(b) implies a = b.
A function is onto if every element of the codomain is an output of some input, so range = codomain.
A constant function gives the same output for every input, for example f(x) = 5.
An identity function maps every x to itself, f(x) = x, and a function can also be shown by a table, a set of pairs, an arrow diagram or a graph.

problem.en: Is f = {(1,4),(2,5),(3,4)} a function from {1,2,3} to {4,5}? Is it one-one? Is it onto?

text.en: Each of 1, 2, 3 appears once as a first element, so f is a function.

why.en: Every input has exactly one output.

text.en: But 1 and 3 both go to 4, so different inputs share an output. f is not one-one.

why.en: One-one needs different outputs for different inputs.

text.en: The outputs used are 4 and 5, which is the whole codomain, so f is onto.

prompt.en: How do you decide whether a relation is a function? Then explain one-one and onto.

requiredIdeas.en: Each input has exactly one output
One-one means different inputs give different outputs

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking two inputs sharing an output breaks the function rule

points.en: A function gives exactly one output for each input.
One-one: no two inputs share an output. Onto: range = codomain.
Constant function f(x) = c; identity function f(x) = x.
Use the vertical line test on graphs.
